title: koinonia
summary: Acts 2:42–47 depicts shared life through teaching, fellowship, meals, prayer, and care for people in need. Ephesians 4 emphasizes unity and the contributions that help a community mature; 1 Peter 2 portrays believers as a spiritual household and people; Hebrews 10 calls for gathering and encouragement. These passages help readers see the communal setting around the term, but the wider references do not all make the same point or necessarily contain the same Greek word.
historical_context: The references include the narrative account of a Jerusalem community in Acts and exhortations in Ephesians, 1 Peter, and Hebrews. The source records provide these biblical contexts but no independent study of ancient associations or the term’s full usage history.
canonical_context: Acts gives the clearest scene of shared practices; Ephesians focuses on unity and mutual contribution; 1 Peter describes common identity; Hebrews emphasizes meeting and encouragement. Read together, they portray community as participation, service, and mutual care rather than merely a gathering at one time or place.
literary_context: Acts narrates practices, Ephesians develops a body metaphor, 1 Peter uses household and peoplehood imagery, and Hebrews exhorts its readers. The literary differences matter: a narrative description, metaphor, and pastoral appeal cannot be collapsed into a single definition.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect shared life with teaching, prayer, care, unity, service, and encouragement. These practices show why communal participation matters in the cited texts, while the exact force of the Greek term in each passage would require lexical evidence not supplied here.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages that portray communal life and participation in distinct ways. It offers contextual examples without claiming that every reference is an occurrence of one word or a complete lexical definition.

interpretive_notes.note: Do not reduce koinonia to a single English gloss.
Check the immediate context and genre before drawing theological conclusions.
